en: So now with that, we're almost ready to get
started downloading and running models on
our system. But before we do that, and
before we take a closer look at the hardware
requirements you have to meet,
it's important to talk about licenses.
Because I mentioned earlier that when using
open large language models, when running
them locally, especially when using them
commercially though,
you must make sure that you respect the
license of the creator, of the provider of
that large language model. So the license
created by
Google for their Gemma models or Meta for
their LLaMA models, for example.
And you can find out which license applies
to a certain model, for example, on Hugging
Face by going to the model card of the model
you're interested in.
And there at the top, you'll typically find
this license
badge here,
which tells you which license applies to
this model. In this case, for this Gemma 3
model I opened as an example here, it's the
Gemma license.
And you can then click on this badge to view
the underlying license file,
which in this case leads us to Google's page
here,
where you can go through that license to
understand how you may and may not use this
model.
And of course, there are many different
licenses out there, but amongst the most
important ones to be aware of are, for
example, the MIT and Apache 2.0 licenses,
which would be very permissive licenses.
And for example, DeepSeek R1 would be one
open model that does use the MIT license.
Now, the MIT license, like the Apache 2.0
license, is very permissive. Commercial use
is no problem there. You just may need to
provide some attribution or extra
information to the users
of your service. Now, many open models,
however, do not use such permissive
licenses. For example, another important
license to be aware of is Meta's LLaMA
license.
This is a somewhat permissive license. It
does allow you to run LLaMA on your system,
on your servers, and it does allow
commercial use, but with certain
limitations. For example, for this Llama 4
license, when commercially using this model,
if you have more than 700 million monthly
active users
at the point of time where this model
version is released, if I read this
correctly, you must request an extra license
from Meta, which they of course may or may
not grant you and for which they of course
may or may not charge money.
In addition, attribution is required and
certain
kinds of use
are prohibited.
Illegal use, for example, but maybe also
some other scenarios. So you definitely need
to check the license agreements to find out
how you may and may not use the LLaMA
models.
The same is true for the Gemma models.
Google has their own license, which is also
somewhat permissive, which does allow
private and commercial use.
And which has no limitations like Meta, at
least at the point of time where I'm
recording this. You don't need to get a
different license once you have a certain
amount of users, but there still are special
requirements regarding attribution, for
example,
or that certain use cases are prohibited.
In general, whenever using an open model,
especially when using it commercially, of
course, you should check the terms and the
license of that model to find out whether
you may use the model the way you want to.
In general, those open models do have quite
permissive licenses, but as explained here,
you should definitely take a closer look,
especially once you plan to use these open
models commercially.
